questions.topic: Reading a two-stage particulate sampler
questions.learningObjective: Identify the two size fractions a two-stage sampler separates
questions.stem: A transit board contractor runs a two-stage particulate sampler beside the depot loading bay. What does the instrument separate?

options.text: It splits airborne particles into a coarse fraction on the first stage and a fine fraction on the second
It measures total suspended particulate twice, so the two stages give a replicate check on one range
options.misconception: assumes both stages collect the same size fraction

options.text: It separates particles by hygroscopic growth, so stage one holds damp dust and stage two holds dry dust
options.misconception: believes the stages separate by moisture not size

options.text: It separates particles by electrical charge, capturing heavier ions first and lighter aerosols second
options.misconception: thinks the stages sort by charge rather than by size

questions.explanation: Two-stage samplers apply two size cuts: stage one traps coarse particles, stage two the fine fraction. Reading both as one repeated range discards the size information the instrument gives.
questions.hint: Ask which stage intercepts the largest particles first.

questions.topic: Why a steady emission gives a varying concentration
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a steady emission yields a varying concentration
questions.stem: Depot vents release particulates at a steady 12 grams per hour all day, yet fence-line monitors read 8, 5, and 19 micrograms per cubic metre at 09:00, 13:00, and 17:00. What best explains the pattern?

options.text: The vents shut down intermittently, so the 13:00 reading reflects a period with no release at all
options.misconception: assumes the source stops rather than diluting

options.text: Concentration depends on wind speed and mixing, so the same steady release spreads over more or less air
The monitors drift upward through the day, so 19 micrograms per cubic metre is an instrument artefact
options.misconception: blames monitor drift instead of dilution

options.text: More staff arrive later, so human dust from the depot yard explains the 17:00 peak
options.misconception: attributes the peak to people rather than air volume

questions.explanation: A steady source gives a concentration set by dilution, the release divided by the air volume it mixes into. Wind and mixing vary through the day, so readings change even though the release does not.
questions.hint: Think about how much air the same release spreads into.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Buffering explains why two catchments differ
questions.learningObjective: Explain how buffering accounts for a difference between catchments
questions.stem: Two neighbouring busway catchments drain similar rainfall volumes, yet one shows fish kills in its stream after a wet spring while the other does not. Explain how buffering accounts for the difference.

answer.exemplar: The catchment underlain by limestone contains carbonate that neutralises hydrogen ions as acid percolates, so runoff leaving it is less acidic and dissolves fewer metals. The catchment on unreactive sandstone has little such capacity, so the same acid load leaves both catchments with low pH and mobilised aluminium that harms aquatic life.

questions.explanation: Buffering capacity sets how much acidity soil and bedrock absorb before the stream turns acid. Limestone neutralises the load, sandstone does not, so identical rainfall gives different chemistry.
questions.hint: Think about which bedrock can neutralise incoming acid.

options.misconception: treats low base saturation as proof of poor drainage

options.text: Base saturation is 75 percent, so the soil is fertile regardless of the exchange capacity value
options.misconception: conflates base saturation with total fertility

options.text: Base saturation is 75 percent, which supports the claim only because the capacity itself is also high
Base saturation is 75 percent, so no further test of the remaining exchange sites is needed
options.misconception: thinks one percentage settles soil fertility

questions.explanation: Base saturation is exchangeable calcium over total capacity, 9 over 12, giving 75 percent. That supports the claim only because the underlying capacity is high as well, not on the percentage alone.
questions.hint: Divide the calcium held by the total sites.

questions.topic: Processes that form two soil horizons
questions.learningObjective: Design a field study of horizon formation in embankment fill
questions.stem: The transit board plans a tree-planting scheme on a new embankment and wants to know which soil-forming processes matter there. Design a field study that would reveal how an O and a B horizon form in the embankment fill.

answer.exemplar: Dig paired pits along and across the embankment and log colour, texture, structure and thickness of each horizon at fixed depths, then date them using buried marker layers of known installation date. Compare weathered fill on the slope crest, which is exposed to air and rain, with buried fill protected from oxygen, and record root density, clay skins and earthworm channels as evidence of biological mixing and eluviation.

questions.explanation: Paired pits, dated marker layers and process-specific measurements let weathering, clay translocation and biological mixing be told apart. Sampling one site would confound position with development.
questions.hint: Include buried markers and a comparison site.

options.text: Dry, loose, unvegetated surface with strong winds, so grains are light and easily entrained

questions.explanation: Wind erosion needs a loose dry surface, little vegetation and wind strong enough to move grains. Water erosion depends on raindrop impact and runoff, so the agents respond to different conditions.
questions.hint: Look for dryness, bare ground and moving air.

questions.topic: Why a steady emission gives a varying concentration
questions.learningObjective: Explain the mechanism linking release rate to concentration
questions.stem: A depot vented at a constant rate still triggers dust complaints on windy afternoons and none on calm days, even though operating hours are identical. Explain the mechanism linking emission rate to measured concentration.

answer.exemplar: Concentration is the release rate spread through the air volume passing the receptor, so a constant emission gives a higher concentration when wind speed is low and mixing is shallow. On windy days the plume is diluted over a much larger volume of air and the measured concentration falls, which is why complaints track wind rather than activity.

questions.explanation: Concentration depends on the volume of air a plume mixes into, not the release rate alone. Stronger wind and deeper mixing dilute a steady source, so complaints track weather rather than operations.
questions.hint: Think about the volume of air carrying the release.

options.misconception: swaps the pathways and picks the wrong dominant one

options.text: Wet deposition carries acid in rainfall and dry deposition carries acid in particles, with wet dominating here
Wet deposition is rainfall only and dry deposition is soil dust only, so neither delivers salt to the stream
options.misconception: treats dry deposition as harmless soil dust

options.text: Both pathways act only through rainfall, so the two labels describe the same process
options.misconception: believes wet and dry deposition are identical

questions.explanation: Wet deposition is acid carried in precipitation, dry deposition is acid in particles settling between showers. Salting releases both, but rainfall scavenging delivers most of the load to the stream.
questions.hint: One pathway uses rain, the other uses particles.

questions.topic: Buffering explains why two catchments differ
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison isolating buffering from rainfall
questions.stem: Two candidate busway corridors drain catchments with very different bedrock. Design a comparison that would show whether buffering, rather than rainfall amount, controls stream acidity.

answer.exemplar: Pair the two catchments and sample stream pH, alkalinity and dissolved metals at the same times over a full year, while recording rainfall in each catchment separately. If acidity differs when rainfall is similar, but alkalinity tracks bedrock, buffering rather than rainfall amount is the controlling factor; a limestone block leached with acid from the same catchment adds a controlled check.

questions.explanation: The design must hold rainfall roughly constant while changing bedrock and must measure alkalinity, so buffering can be told apart from dilution. Sampling one catchment alone would confound the causes.
questions.hint: Pair catchments and measure alkalinity, not just pH.

options.text: Cation exchange capacity measures how much nitrogen a soil can hold at once, so it predicts fertility directly
options.misconception: confuses exchange capacity with nitrogen supply

options.text: Total nutrient content is irrelevant because plants draw all their nutrients from the soil solution
options.misconception: believes solution nutrients are the only supply

options.text: Exchange capacity sets how many cations soil retains against leaching, so added nutrients stay available
Cation exchange capacity only affects clay texture, so it says nothing about how long nutrients persist
options.misconception: treats exchange capacity as a texture proxy only

questions.explanation: Cations on exchange sites resist leaching, so high exchange capacity retains added nutrients while low capacity loses them. Total content alone says nothing about how long the supply lasts.
questions.hint: Think about whether added nutrients stay put.

options.misconception: ties clay skins to wind instead of water

questions.learningObjective: Assess a replacement claim against incomplete records
questions.stem: The quarry operator tells the board that the site replaces every tonne of stone it removes. Records show 9000 tonnes extracted, 8600 tonnes sold as aggregate and 1200 tonnes sold as dust filler. Assess the claim.

answer.exemplar: Material left the site as aggregate and as dust filler, and both count as products rather than waste, so the claim rests on treating all output as replacement. The board should ask what became of overburden, fines and fines left as spoil, because replacing only the sold fraction ignores the material that never became product at all.

questions.explanation: The claim is only as good as the definition of replacement, and the records omit the 900 tonnes difference between extraction and sale plus unsold spoil. A balance must account for every tonne.

questions.stem: Design a field trial that would show whether measured particulate concentration near the depot depends on wind speed rather than on the emission rate.

answer.exemplar: Operate the sampler at a fixed height with the depot vents held at a constant measured release rate, then record concentration together with wind speed and atmospheric stability at the same site across many days. If concentration falls as wind speed rises while release stays fixed, dilution is the cause; if concentration tracks release instead, the source rate explains the variation.

questions.explanation: The trial must hold the source constant and vary the meteorology, recording wind and concentration together at one site. If release is not controlled, wind and emission rate stay confounded.

questions.stem: The same gravel shoulder design was stable on the western half of the busway and eroded on the eastern half, where the surface was finer and less vegetated. Explain what governs the choice between wind and water erosion there.

answer.exemplar: Erosion by water is driven by raindrop impact and overland flow, so it grows where the surface is fine enough to be detached and sealed and where runoff concentrates; erosion by wind needs loose, dry, unvegetated grains that strong winds can entrain. The eastern shoulder was fine-textured and bare, so it lost material to splash and runoff, while the coarse vegetated western shoulder resisted both agents.

questions.explanation: The two agents respond to different properties: water needs detachable fines and runoff, wind needs loose dry grains and bare ground. The finer, unvegetated eastern shoulder fell to water erosion.

questions.stem: A limestone quarry catchment keeps its stream near pH 7 while a neighbouring sandstone catchment drops to pH 4 after heavy rain. Explain how buffering accounts for the difference in a way the board can present to the public.

answer.exemplar: Rainwater carries weak acids dissolved from the atmosphere and from soil organic matter, and this load has to be neutralised somewhere before it reaches the stream. questions.explanation: Carbonate in limestone consumes hydrogen ions as soil water percolates, so the quarry catchment exports near-neutral water. Sandstone has no such reaction, so acid reaches the stream unchanged.

options.misconception: ignores base saturation when computing calcium

options.text: Exchangeable calcium is 1.2 centimoles per kilogram, so the on-site soil is far too poor to use
options.misconception: subtracts base saturation from exchange capacity

options.misconception: treats one calculation as a complete fertility verdict

questions.explanation: Base saturation is the share of exchange sites holding calcium, so 60 percent of 8 is 4.8 centimoles per kilogram. That supports part of the claim, but moderate capacity leaves the soil leachable.

questions.topic: Processes that form two soil horizons
questions.learningObjective: Design a survey for horizon recognition
questions.stem: The board wants to know whether a candidate fill site has distinct A and B horizons or only one uniform layer. Design a survey that would test this.

answer.exemplar: Dig pits at several points across the site and log colour, texture, structure, organic matter and boundary sharpness at 10 centimetre intervals down the profile, using a spade and auger where pits are impractical. Repeat on the highest and lowest ground so that any horizons found can be separated from depth differences, and record whether boundaries are gradual or sharp.

questions.explanation: Horizon recognition needs descriptions at fixed intervals from several places, including a contrast in elevation, so one colour change is not a boundary. A single pit cannot establish a pattern.
questions.hint: Log many depths and compare high and low ground.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a steady emission gives a varying concentration
questions.learningObjective: Explain the two-part reasoning behind a changed reading
questions.stem: A depot wall sensor records the same hourly release as yesterday, but the fence monitor reads twice yesterday's value. Explain the two-part reasoning that produces this outcome.

answer.exemplar: The monitor measures a concentration, not a release, and concentration is the release divided by the volume of air carrying it. If the release is unchanged but the reading doubles, the air volume available for mixing must have halved, most likely because wind dropped and the mixing layer became shallower. The instrument therefore reflects dilution as much as source strength.

questions.explanation: A concentration depends on release and air volume, so an unchanged release with a doubled reading means the plume mixed into half as much air. Treating the monitor as a source meter misdiagnoses it.
questions.hint: Separate source strength from dilution in the reading.

options.misconception: reverses the two pathway names

options.misconception: assumes liming removes airborne acidity

questions.explanation: Damage that follows dry windy spells points to acid carried on settled particles, the dry pathway, rather than acid arriving in rain. Liming changes the soil, not the air reaching the crop.
questions.hint: Match the damage timing to the pathway.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Buffering explains why two catchments differ
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison of bedrock and soil buffering
questions.stem: Design a way to estimate how much of a catchment's acid-neutralising capacity comes from bedrock rather than from soil organic matter.

answer.exemplar: Collect paired soil and weathered bedrock samples from the same profiles and titrate each for exchangeable bases and for carbonate content, then compare the base-richness of soils formed on the two bedrock types. If the limestone-derived soils hold far more exchangeable calcium and magnesium than the sandstone-derived soils over comparable rainfall and land use, the difference in buffering is attributable to bedrock, while the soil itself contributes relatively little.

questions.explanation: To separate the two sources, buffering must be measured on soils formed on different bedrocks under comparable rainfall and land use. Measuring soil alone would leave bedrock untested.
questions.hint: Compare soils formed on different bedrocks.

questions.hint: Availability, not inventory, drives plant uptake.

questions.topic: A replenishment claim that a balance contradicts
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a surplus balance can coexist with rising imports
questions.stem: The board's briefing claims the gravel yard's material balance shows no net depletion, yet imports of fresh aggregate have risen for three years running. Explain how the balance can show a surplus while the yard still depends on new material.

answer.exemplar: A balance that counts only the yard's own stock sees inflows equal to outflows and closes on itself, which is why it can report a surplus while the picture of the wider system changes. Fresh imports rising year on year show that demand for the material is growing faster than the recovered or stockpiled supply, so the yard is drawing on reserves that the closed account never records as a loss.

questions.explanation: A closed stock account can balance while wider flows grow, because rising demand shows up as higher imports rather than a stock deficit. The balance answers a narrower question than the board asks.
questions.hint: Ask where the extra new material is going.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a steady emission gives a varying concentration
questions.learningObjective: Design a study separating stack and resuspended sources
questions.stem: Design an approach to establish whether the depot's measured particulate concentration is dominated by emissions or by particles resuspended from the yard.

answer.exemplar: Run paired sampling periods with the depot on normal duty and again with the yard surface swept and wetted or the loading bay sealed, keeping the samplers in the same positions and the same wind conditions as far as possible. A marked drop in concentration during the resuspension-control periods identifies the yard as a major source, whereas little change points to the vent stack, and a tracer gas released at the stack can confirm the split.

questions.explanation: Sources can only be separated by changing one suspected source while holding the rest steady, so controlled periods with the yard treated matter. Sampling the stack and the yard assigns the mass.
questions.hint: Change one suspected source and watch the reading.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Conditions for erosion by wind and by water
questions.learningObjective: Explain the diagnostic checks for erosion control
questions.stem: A transit planner wants a rule of thumb for choosing between wind erosion control and water erosion control on a proposed shoulder. Explain the diagnostic checks that should decide the choice.

answer.exemplar: The check for water erosion is whether raindrops can detach the surface particles and whether runoff concentrates: fine-textured, sealed or crusted surfaces with long unbroken slopes and sparse cover are the classic targets, and the remedy is cover, contouring and drainage. The check for wind erosion is whether grains are dry, loose and bare with winds strong enough to move them, and the remedy is surface crusting, anchoring and windbreaks. Doing both costs more than diagnosing first.

questions.explanation: The two processes leave different evidence: splash rills and concentrated runoff point to water, drifting sand and deflation to wind. Choosing controls before identifying the agent wastes money.
questions.hint: Look for rills for water and drift for wind.

questions.stem: The board wants a defensible test that the busway project's recycled content claim is real rather than a bookkeeping convention.

answer.exemplar: Specify the claim precisely as a mass or volume fraction, then verify it independently by requiring chain-of-custody records for delivered material, spot checks of the delivered tonnage against weighbridge tickets and audit sampling of the stockpile itself. Because the figures come from the contractor's own documents, an audit by a party with no supply interest gives the board a check that the claim is more than a definition.

questions.explanation: A vague claim cannot be tested, so it must be restated as a quantity with a stated denominator. Independent auditing matters because the contractor's own records would be both claim and evidence.
questions.hint: Restate the claim, then verify it independently.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why bedrock alone does not guarantee clear streams
questions.stem: A board paper claims the corridor's streams are clear because the catchment sits on granite. Explain why that claim does not follow from the geology alone.

answer.exemplar: Granite is not alkaline, so it supplies little carbonate to neutralise acid; the rock may even weather to release acidity. A stream can also receive hydrogen ions from atmospheric deposition and from the oxidation of sulphur in the soil, and a catchment with organic soils and poor drainage can export more acid than its rock alone would predict. Geology is one term in the budget, not the whole of it.

questions.explanation: Acid comes from deposition and the soil as well as the rock, and granite contributes little base, so rock type alone cannot guarantee clear streams. Saturated organic soils export acidity.
questions.hint: Think about acid sources outside the bedrock.

answer.exemplar: Expose a fresh pit face through the full profile and describe structure, colour, clay skins, stone shape and the presence of roots or worm channels, then compare the same features in a pit on a mature adjacent field. questions.explanation: Horizon recognition rests on structure, clay skins and stone weathering compared against parent material, so the test must compare rather than rely on colour. A mature-field pit is the reference.

questions.explanation: Audited delivery of 900 against 2600 tonnes used is 34.6 percent. The claim of 1400 tonnes implies 53.8 percent, so documented material supports a smaller share than advertised.
questions.hint: Divide audited tonnes by total tonnes used.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading a two-stage particulate sampler
questions.learningObjective: Convert sampled flow, duration and mass into a concentration
questions.stem: A depot sampler runs at 1.5 cubic metres per minute for 8 hours and the combined mass collected on both stages is 5040 milligrams. What is the measured concentration in milligrams per cubic metre?
questions.explanation: Eight hours at 1.5 cubic metres per minute gives 720 cubic metres of air sampled. The combined 5040 milligrams divided by 720 cubic metres gives 7 milligrams per cubic metre.
questions.hint: Multiply flow by minutes, then divide mass by volume.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a steady emission gives a varying concentration
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two depots with equal fleets differ
questions.stem: Two depots on the same corridor, with identical vehicle fleets and hours, show fence concentrations that differ by a factor of four. Explain the reasoning that accounts for the difference.

answer.exemplar: Identical fleets and hours fix the release, so the difference has to lie in how each plume is diluted or how much dust each yard adds. The busier depot may push its exhaust through a narrow lane between sheds, where the plume has less room to mix before reaching the fence, while the open depot disperses the same release across a wide volume of air. Comparing wind records and site layouts at the two depots tests that explanation.

questions.explanation: Equal fleets and hours mean equal release, so the contrast points to dilution or resuspended yard dust rather than engine output. Comparing layout and wind records tests which mechanism operates.
questions.hint: Hold the fleet constant and look at the plume path.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The two pathways of acid deposition
questions.learningObjective: Identify both routes by which gas-phase acid reaches the ground
questions.stem: A catchment receives nitrogen oxides from traffic and power stations, which become nitric acid in the air. First name the wet and dry pathways for its deposition, then say which route carries gas-phase acid to the ground.

options.text: The wet pathway carries dry particles and the dry pathway carries rainfall, so the labels are reversed
options.misconception: reverses the two deposition pathway names

options.text: Wet deposition carries dissolved nitric acid in rain, while dry deposition carries it on particles
Only the wet pathway applies, because gas-phase acids are washed out before particles can carry them
options.misconception: excludes dry deposition for gas-phase acids

options.text: Neither pathway applies, because nitric acid in the atmosphere is too dilute to be deposited
options.misconception: believes dilute acids cannot be deposited

questions.explanation: Gas-phase nitric acid is removed from the air both dissolved in precipitation and adsorbed onto settling particles, so both pathways operate. Excluding either would underestimate the deposition.
questions.hint: Both wet and dry routes carry gas-phase acid.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Buffering explains why two catchments differ
questions.learningObjective: Design a monitoring plan for a catchment amendment
questions.stem: The board needs a monitoring plan that can demonstrate whether a new limestone amendment to a busway catchment actually improves stream acidity over time.

answer.exemplar: Establish a before-and-after design with a control catchment on similar soils and bedrock, and record stream pH, alkalinity, base cations and flow at fixed points, monthly at minimum and through at least one full wet season, together with rainfall and any road salting on the treated catchment. Success means a rising alkalinity and base cation concentration in the amended catchment relative to the control, with pH rising only once the base supply has exceeded the acid load.

questions.explanation: The plan needs a time series, a control and mass-balance indicators, because one set of pH readings after liming would confound treatment with seasonal change. Base cations show whether it works.
questions.hint: Include a control and repeat sampling over time.
